||You are twittering very much, police said Social media Twittering opponents azc should expect a visit from the police. Is it allowed?||

Monday afternoon Mark Jongeneel (28) received a disturbing phone call. His mother called. There had just been two policemen at the door who were looking for him, but did not tell why. Now they were on their way to Young Neels office; He has a collection agency. What could be the problem? "Was I drunk Saturday night, shot through my head." But he could remember everything.

"You tweet a lot," said the agents according Jongeneel when they were seated in his office. "We have orders to ask you to watch your tone. Your tweets may seem like incitement."

Tuesday there was a meeting in Sliedrecht about a refugee center in the region. In the run-up to it Jongeneel posted a few tweets.

This one for example: "The College of #Sliedrecht comes with a proposal to deal with over the next two years 250 refugees. What a bad idea! #KominVerzet(ComeIntoProtest) "Earlier he also wrote:" we can't just allow this to happen!? "

|Police state|

In recent months, police has visited many more people at home who spoke up against asylum centers on social media. In October there were 20 more home visits in Leeuwarden about opponents of azc programs. And in Enschede local policemen visited sympathizers of AZC alert Enschede. In the Brabant Kaatsheuvel at least three villagers had home visits from the police because they critisized the arrival of an emergency shelter or because they ran a page of that topic on social media.

With these visits, the police are trying to persuade the citizens' "what effect a post or tweet on the internet can have", said a spokesman for the National Police. Using ten real-time intelligence units digital detectives groups spread across the country, Facebook pages and Twitter accounts are monitored. It looks for posts that go "too far".

Municipalities send the police as well. That happened for Jongeneel. The spokesman of the municipality Sliedrecht explains that they wanted to make it clear that any physical demonstration "good" is, but it must be reported to the municipality. "It was definitely not the intention to shut him up. Really. We believe that everyone should be able to voice his opinion." It did not come across as freely to Jongeneel. "It's as if we're living in a police state."

|Freedom of speech|

"Those assholes should fuck off, we're all going to the town hall", posted mechanic Johan van Wouw (43) a few weeks ago on a Monday morning on his own Facebook page. Shortly before he read on the Internet 1200 refugees would be placed at Kaatsheuvel and wanted to let on that he did not agree with that. Later that afternoon police at his door. "They thought I incited a demonstration and demanded that I removed the post from the internet."

The visit lasted about twenty minutes and the police behaved quite authoritarian, Van Wouw found. Since then he feels as if his freedom is restricted. "When I now post something on Facebook, I realize that the police might be reading along."

|Hate speech| Other people who got police to visits, felt that they were being gagged. "Why can not we say what we think?" Asks Kim (33) from Kaatsheuvel. She does not want her last name in the newspaper. Kim got police at the door because of tweets from her and her boyfriend. She posted several Facebook messages showing their discontent for a reception center in the neighborhood. Things like: "Is this place going to end up like Geldermalsen? Kim: "But aren't the people who act on these posts the ones doing wrong?"

Hate speech or incitement is prohibited in the Netherlands. But when is this limit overstepped? According to the spokesman of the National Police it is very difficult to say. New estimates are made regularly; there are no specific rules.

"It is a subtle boundary that can easily be overstepped" said law professor Nico Kwakman, affiliated with the University of Groningen. "You are allowed to say, 'I think Islam an outdated, backwater religion." That is an opinion. But if you go on to say: "Muslims are evil and should be re-educated", you overstep a boundary " It also depends on the moment of the remark..

Basically this also shows the police is getting with the times, says Jaap Timmer, associate professor of social security at the Free University in Amsterdam. "Back in the day, if someone in a cafe would say he would go on a demonstration and break some windows, that person would get a home visit. The police have apparently discovered that the public domain is also happening on social media. "

|Again not taken seriously|

"The policeman is seen as someone who detects crime, but also to prevent crime, to advise/consult citizens and help," said criminal justice expert Kwakman. I believe that is what the police intended in cases like these. "But it has been, I think, severely underestimated what it means for the individual." According to Kwakman it would have been more prudent to send an official, one without police uniform. "If a policeman comes to your door to telling you what you're doing is wrong, you feel slighted and criminalized."

The police visit in Kaatsheuvel only made Kim angrier, she says. "The municipality is taking so much effort to make sure that we keep our mouths shut, what does that mean?"
